newsitem.title: GERMANY: German coffee trade sees sideways price trend.
newsitem.headline: German coffee trade sees sideways price trend.

text.p: Coffee prices are vulnerable after selling bouts last week, but tight supply and winter buying by roasters may provide enough support to keep them steady, German traders said on Monday.
"It's hard to say -- funds are long in New York and robusta prices may ease seasonally," one said.
"But that doesn't mean the right coffee reaches the buyer in Europe. Quality arabicas may be tight for months on end and this can't just be reflected via differentials."
He saw little scope for the December premium over March in New York -- 8.75 cents/lb at Friday's close -- to ease.

Physical market sources said Central American new crop imports were not looking too comfortable for first quarter 1997 and this could mean December strength may be rolled into March on the futures markets.
Differentials were firm as Central American origin sellers competed with each other for high earnings.
Only Brazilian exporters continued to buck the trend and reduced differentials.
Roaster cover in Germany was described as adequate in the first quarter and thinner in the months beyond that.
But a week or two into the European winter, markets were also preparing for possible seasonal consumption rises.
Traders said the second half of the 1996/97 season looked more comfortable because new crops would have been put into stores by then.
In addition, Colombia might need to sell national stocks to secure revenue in a continuing infrastructure and earnings crisis.
Markets were looking for direction from first Brazilian 1997/98 estimates due to be released this week or in early December.
Outright arabica prices were marked down on the week by $3-4.50 per 50 kg fob, with the exception of Kenyans, which were $9 higher.
Colombia Excelso was at $136 and Brazils at $108.50 while Indonesian robustas eased $1 to $63.50 for Dec/Jan cif.
